title: Learning How to Learn
subtitle: The evidence behind retrieval, spacing and self-explanation, and how this app uses it
overview: Before the HAI material, spend an hour or two on how durable learning actually happens. Decades of cognitive-psychology research converge on a few techniques that work: retrieving from memory, spacing that retrieval over days and weeks, and explaining ideas in your own words. Comfortable techniques like rereading or relistening work poorly. Every feature in this app is built around that research: prequestions, recall pauses while you listen, free recall after each source, confidence-rated check-ins, and a spaced daily review. This stage shows you the evidence so you know why the app asks you to do slightly harder things.

modules.title: What makes learning stick
modules.goal: Explain why retrieval practice and spacing beat rereading, and why the feeling of fluency is a poor guide to what you have learned.
modules.guide: Start with Weinstein, Madan & Sumeracki, a short open-access overview of six strategies with strong evidence. Then read Carpenter, Pan & Butler's review, which goes deeper on the two strongest: spacing and retrieval practice. Roediger & Karpicke (2006) is the classic experiment behind the 'testing effect'. Look at how results 5 minutes later differ from results a week later. Key terms: 'retrieval practice' (pulling information out of memory, e.g. by answering questions, rather than putting it back in by rereading); 'spacing' (spreading practice over time instead of cramming); 'desirable difficulty' (a learning condition that feels harder and slower but produces better long-term retention); 'fluency illusion' (mistaking how easily something feels familiar right now for how well you will remember it later).

resources.title: Teaching the science of learning
resources.why: A compact, open-access tour of the six learning strategies with the strongest evidence: spaced practice, interleaving, retrieval practice, elaboration, concrete examples and dual coding. Each comes with a note on how to use it.
resources.focus: Read the sections on each of the six strategies; skim the discussion of the gap between research and teaching practice.

resources.title: The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice
resources.why: A current, authoritative review of the two techniques with the largest and most replicated effects, including why learners underuse them. These two techniques drive the daily review in this app.
resources.focus: Focus on how spacing and retrieval practice work, and the section on why learners misjudge them. Skim the classroom-implementation details.

resources.title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
resources.why: The landmark experiment showing that taking a test is not just measurement: it changes memory. It also shows how a short-term advantage for restudying can mislead you.
resources.focus: Compare the results at 5 minutes, 2 days and 1 week, and note what students predicted about their own learning.

resources.title: Improving Students’ Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
resources.venue: Psychological Science in the Public Interest
resources.why: The most-cited evaluation of ten common study techniques. It rated each for utility across learners, materials and tasks. It is why rereading and highlighting are considered weak strategies.
resources.focus: Read the introduction, the summary table of utility ratings, and the sections on practice testing and distributed practice. Skim the others.

resources.title: Retrieval Practice Produces More Learning than Elaborative Studying with Concept Mapping
resources.why: Free recall (writing down everything you remember) beat an active, elaborate study method, even on inference questions. This is the basis for the free-recall step after each source in this app.

resources.title: Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence
resources.venue: Psychological Science in the Public Interest
resources.why: A careful look at the popular idea that teaching should match your 'learning style'. Useful both for your own studying and as a model of what evidence for a claim like this would need to look like.
resources.focus: Focus on the section describing the experimental design needed to support the meshing hypothesis.

quiz.q: In Roediger & Karpicke (2006), students either restudied a prose passage or took recall tests on it. What happened?
choices: Testing won at every delay, including 5 minutes later
Restudying won at 5 minutes, but testing led to much better retention after 2 days and 1 week
The two conditions were equivalent at every delay
Restudying won at every delay because students saw the material more times
quiz.explain: Restudying gave a small advantage on the immediate test, but the tested groups retained much more after 2 days and 1 week. Students who only restudied were also more confident about their learning. Source: Roediger & Karpicke 2006.

quiz.q: Which two techniques did Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate as having high utility?
choices: Highlighting and summarization
Rereading and the keyword mnemonic
Practice testing and distributed practice
Imagery for text and interleaved practice
quiz.explain: Practice testing and distributed (spaced) practice were the only two rated high utility. Interleaving, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation were moderate. Rereading, highlighting, summarization, the keyword mnemonic and imagery for text were rated low. Source: Dunlosky et al. 2013.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six strategies covered by Weinstein, Madan & Sumeracki (2018)?
choices: Dual coding
Interleaving
Concrete examples
Matching instruction to each student's learning style
quiz.explain: The six are spaced practice, interleaving, retrieval practice, elaboration, concrete examples and dual coding. Matching instruction to learning styles is a popular idea without supporting evidence (see Pashler et al. 2008). Source: Weinstein et al. 2018.

quiz.q: You have just listened to a paper twice in a row and it now feels very familiar. Based on the reviews in this module, what is the best interpretation?
choices: The familiarity proves the material is in long-term memory
Familiarity right after massed study is a poor predictor of later retention, so test yourself after a delay
You should listen a third time to be safe
Feeling of knowing is a reliable guide as long as you were paying attention
quiz.explain: Massed re-exposure creates fluency, which learners mistake for durable learning. Carpenter, Pan & Butler describe how this metacognitive illusion leads people to underuse spacing and retrieval, even though those techniques produce better long-term retention.

quiz.q: Karpicke & Blunt (2011) compared retrieval practice with elaborative concept mapping. Which statement matches their findings?
choices: Concept mapping won on inference questions, retrieval practice only on verbatim questions
Both methods were equally effective
Retrieval practice produced more learning on both verbatim and inference questions, even though students predicted otherwise
Retrieval practice only helped students who already had high prior knowledge
quiz.explain: Retrieval practice (free recall) beat concept mapping on verbatim and inference questions a week later, even when the final test was itself a concept map. Students' predictions about which method would work best were wrong. Source: Karpicke & Blunt 2011.

quiz.q: According to Pashler et al. (2008), what evidence would be needed to support the learning-styles 'meshing' hypothesis?
choices: A survey showing that most people have a preferred learning style
A crossover interaction: learners of style A learn best with method A, and learners of style B learn best with method B
Any study showing that visual materials improve learning
Students reporting that they enjoy materials matched to their style
quiz.explain: Pashler et al. argue that the hypothesis needs a specific crossover interaction in a randomized design. They found very few studies with that design, and those that existed did not support the hypothesis. Preference and enjoyment are not evidence of better learning.

modules.exercise: Think about how you studied for your hardest CS course. List the techniques you used (rereading notes, redoing problems, flashcards, highlighting…) and place each on Dunlosky et al.'s utility scale. Then write down one specific change you will make while working through this path. For example: 'after each source I will write down everything I remember before looking at my notes'.

modules.title: The techniques built into this app
modules.goal: Explain the evidence for each learning feature in the app: prequestions, interpolated recall, confidence ratings, successive relearning, and spaced, interleaved review.
modules.guide: Each paper here backs one feature you will meet in the app. Prequestions are the 'Before you start' questions on each module (Pan & Carpenter): you commit to a guess before learning, and the answer is not shown until the check-in. Recall pauses at section breaks while listening follow Szpunar et al.'s interpolated tests. The confidence rating on every quiz answer uses the hypercorrection effect (Butterfield & Metcalfe): confident errors, once corrected, tend to stick. The daily review uses successive relearning (Rawson & Dunlosky): missed items come back in the same session until you get them right, then return over spaced sessions. Latimier et al.'s meta-analysis is why the schedule spaces retrieval out without fussing over the exact interval formula. Chi et al. is the evidence for the 'explain it in your own words' prompts. Terms: 'interpolated test' (a short quiz inserted partway through a lesson); 'criterion' (the number of correct recalls required before stopping practice on an item).

resources.title: Interpolated memory tests reduce mind wandering and improve learning of online lectures
resources.why: Short tests between segments of a recorded lecture kept learners on task and improved final performance. This is the basis for the recall pauses at section breaks while you listen to papers.

resources.title: Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects: a Review of Empirical Research, Theoretical Perspectives, and Implications for Educational Practice
resources.why: Answering questions before you have learned the material, even incorrectly, improves later learning of that material. This review covers when the effect holds, and it is why every module opens with prequestions.
resources.focus: Read the overview of findings, the section on what prequestions do and don't benefit, and the practical recommendations.

resources.title: Optimizing schedules of retrieval practice for durable and efficient learning: How much is enough?
resources.why: Introduces successive relearning: practice until you recall correctly, then relearn in later spaced sessions. This is the structure of the daily review.
resources.focus: Read the introduction and general discussion; skim the individual experiments.

resources.title: Errors committed with high confidence are hypercorrected.
resources.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
resources.why: Explains why the app asks how sure you are before revealing an answer, and why it flags confident mistakes.

resources.title: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention
resources.why: Quantifies how much spacing adds to retrieval practice and tests whether expanding intervals beat equal ones. That matters for how the review scheduler is designed.

resources.title: Eliciting Self‐Explanations Improves Understanding
resources.why: Prompting learners to explain each line of a text to themselves improved understanding of a complex system. This is the basis for the explain-in-your-own-words prompts.

quiz.q: In Szpunar, Khan & Schacter (2013), what did short tests inserted between segments of an online lecture do?
choices: Increased anxiety and hurt final performance
Reduced mind wandering, increased note-taking and improved learning
Helped only for the tested segments, with no effect on attention
Had no measurable effect compared with restudying the slides
quiz.explain: Interpolated tests reduced mind wandering and increased note-taking. They also improved performance on the final cumulative test, and test anxiety went down rather than up. Source: Szpunar et al. 2013.

quiz.q: Pan & Carpenter's review of prequestioning concludes that the benefit of answering questions before learning is…
choices: Strongest for the specific information the prequestions asked about, with weaker or inconsistent benefits for other material
Equally large for all material in the lesson
Only present when learners guess correctly
Only present for multiple-choice prequestions
quiz.explain: Prequestions reliably improve learning of the prequestioned information, even when the initial guesses are wrong. Benefits for non-prequestioned material are much less consistent. The app therefore uses prequestions drawn from the check-in itself.

quiz.q: What is 'successive relearning' as described by Rawson & Dunlosky?
choices: Rereading a text several times in one sitting
Practising retrieval until you recall each item correctly, then relearning the items to criterion in later spaced sessions
Studying related topics one after another
Learning material once and testing it once a month later
quiz.explain: Successive relearning combines retrieval to a criterion within a session with spacing across sessions. Rawson & Dunlosky found that additional relearning sessions were very effective for durable retention, while extra correct recalls in the first session gave diminishing returns.

choices: People over-correct their answers and change right answers to wrong ones
Errors made with high confidence are more likely to be corrected after feedback than low-confidence errors
Feedback only helps when the original answer was a guess
Confident answers are almost always correct
quiz.explain: Butterfield & Metcalfe found that when people learn the right answer after a high-confidence error, they are more likely to remember the correction than after a low-confidence error. This is why the app asks for confidence and highlights confident mistakes.

quiz.q: Latimier, Peyre & Ramus's meta-analysis compared spaced and massed retrieval practice, and expanding and uniform spacing schedules. What did they find?
choices: Massed retrieval was as good as spaced retrieval
Spaced retrieval beat massed retrieval, but expanding schedules were not reliably better than uniform ones
Only expanding schedules produced any benefit
Spacing helped only for vocabulary learning
quiz.explain: Spacing retrieval episodes produced a substantial benefit over massed retrieval. The difference between expanding and uniform spacing was not significant. The main lesson is to space your retrieval at all; the exact formula matters much less.

quiz.q: You finish a section of a paper on RLHF. Which follow-up activity best applies the research in this stage?
choices: Immediately relisten to the section at a faster speed
Highlight the key sentences in the text
Without looking, explain the section's main idea and why it works in your own words, then check against the text
Move on immediately, since stopping breaks your concentration
quiz.explain: Explaining the material from memory combines retrieval practice with self-explanation (Chi et al. 1994; Szpunar et al. 2013), and checking afterwards gives you feedback. Relistening and highlighting are low-utility, fluency-building activities.

modules.exercise: Design your own learning routine for this path. Decide (1) how many days a week you'll do the daily review and at what time, (2) the maximum number of new sources you'll start per day so reviews stay manageable, and (3) what you'll do on the free-recall screen: type, dictate, or say it out loud. Write it down here and revisit it after two weeks. Did you stick with it, and did the review questions feel easier?
